openers.regulation-and-standards: Before economists offered prices, governments wrote rules. This chapter covers the body of law built to protect the environment, from international treaties and national statutes down to local zoning. It looks at how societies study a project's likely effects before deciding to go ahead, and at the US law of 1973 meant to stop extinctions caused by growth that ignored conservation. Strict rules have side effects too: protecting a species can make it a financial burden for the landowner who hosts it. Running through it all is a set of guiding ideas, such as prevention and equity, that not everyone accepts.

reviews.regulation-and-standards: Environmental law grew from the weak protection of private nuisance suits into a vast body of rules. Its workhorse has been command and control: emission standards, technology standards such as best available technology, and laws like the Clean Air Act and the Clean Water Act, which worked well for point sources but struggled with diffuse pollution. Assessments bring environmental effects into decisions before they are made, while liability laws such as Superfund make polluters pay afterwards. Every tool has drawn dispute, from the perverse incentives of species protection to the delays of NEPA reviews. Underneath sits one long argument: whether direct rules or economic incentives protect the environment more cheaply.

nature-pol-140.title: Environmental law: the rules that protect nature
nature-pol-140.text: London's Great Smog of 1952 changed British law. It led to a 1956 clean-air statute that set emission limits for households and businesses, enforced by an inspectorate. That is environmental law at work. It is the body of treaties, statutes, regulations and policies meant to protect the natural environment. It also manages how human activity affects ecosystems and the resources nature provides. Before such laws, the main protection was the old common-law idea of nuisance. It allowed only private lawsuits when someone's land was harmed, and it proved inadequate for threats to shared resources. Modern environmental law covers {{ref:nature-found-079}} control, resource conservation, biodiversity protection, cutting climate change and {{ref:nature-eecon-209}}. Pollution laws deal with air and water quality, waste, contaminant cleanup and chemical safety. Resource laws govern water, minerals, forests, wildlife, and fish and game. None of it is settled. Regulated industries commonly argue against rules on grounds of cost, while many environmental groups say current rules are too weak. Smaller firms can bear disproportionately large costs, which can keep new firms out. Debates continue over whether regulation is necessary, fair and worth its cost, and whether rules or market solutions better reach agreed goals.

nature-pol-132.title: Environmental impact assessment: look before you build
nature-pol-132.text: More than 180 countries ask the same question before big projects go ahead: what will this do to the environment? An environmental impact assessment (EIA) is a study of the likely environmental effects of a project, plan or policy, done before anyone decides whether to proceed. Its aim is to make sure decision-makers take those effects into account. An EIA does not demand a particular outcome. It requires decision-makers to weigh environmental values and justify their choice, using studies and public comments. EIAs began in the 1960s amid growing environmental awareness. In the United States they gained formal status with the {{ref:nature-pol-168}} of 1969. Today they are a widely used tool of {{ref:nature-gov-117}} worldwide. The process can also look back. At the end of a project, an audit can compare actual impacts with predicted ones, testing the predictions and how well mitigation worked. Gaps remain. Few national EIA laws explicitly require assessing a project's contribution to climate change. EIA is also where {{ref:nature-mkt-119}} is often applied, guided by the {{ref:nature-mkt-130}}.

nature-pol-159.title: The Endangered Species Act of 1973
nature-pol-159.text: On December 28, 1973, the United States signed one of its most powerful, and most controversial, environmental laws. The Endangered Species Act set out to stop extinctions caused by economic growth that ignored conservation. Its two aims are to prevent extinction and to recover species until they no longer need the law's protection. Agencies list species as 'endangered' or the lesser 'threatened'. Section 9 then bans 'take', meaning to harass, harm or hunt them. Since 1982, listing decisions must rest solely on biological and trade information, without weighing economic effects. Because habitat loss is the main threat to most imperiled species, agencies can designate 'critical habitat' zones. By August 2023, 1,780 species had been listed. Of those, 99% were still alive, but only 64 had recovered enough to leave the list. The American alligator, listed in 1967, was delisted as fully recovered twenty years later. The Act also underpins US {{ref:nature-mkt-127}}. Its economic costs keep it in dispute.

nature-pol-168.title: NEPA: the law that made agencies look first
nature-pol-168.text: {{ref:nature-hist-006}}, the 1969 Santa Barbara oil spill and protests against highway building all fed the mood that produced it. The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), passed in 1969 and in force from January 1, 1970, requires federal agencies to weigh environmental effects before acting. It also created the Council on Environmental Quality. Agencies follow three levels of review. The lightest is a categorical exclusion. The middle is an environmental assessment ending in a finding of no significant impact. The heaviest is a full {{ref:nature-pol-133}}. A federal study of 2013-2018 found a full review took 4.5 years on average. The Council has no enforcement power, so violations go through the courts, where the usual remedy is ordering the review redone. NEPA shaped impact assessment in countries such as Australia, and it is the law most used in US climate litigation, with 322 cases filed. Evidence on its costs and benefits is limited. Defenders see a key safeguard that curbed some of the worst abuses; critics blame it for long delays.

nature-pol-177.title: Zoning: deciding what goes where
nature-pol-177.text: Whether a field can become a factory is usually decided by a town, not a nation. Zoning is a way for a local government to divide land into zones. Each zone has its own rules on what may be built and how land may be used, a limit on {{ref:nature-econ-621}}. Zones may allow a single use, such as housing or industry, or mix compatible uses. Form-based zoning governs building size and shape whatever the use. Single-use zoning separates uses thought incompatible, and in practice it also protects existing uses and a community's character. Overlay zones add rules for a particular concern, such as wetlands or a natural hazard, without rewriting the whole code. Zoning is a key tool for helping cities adapt to climate change and manage floods. It also draws fire. Environmental activists argue that separating everyday uses forces car ownership and adds traffic. Some economists say it reduces efficiency and raises housing costs; one 2017 study estimated large GDP gains from partial deregulation. Supporters reply that it is essential for keeping harmful uses apart.

nature-pol-169.title: Natura 2000: Europe's web of protected places
nature-pol-169.text: In 2022, more than 18% of the European Union's land and more than 7% of its marine area sat inside a single network. Natura 2000 is the EU's network of protected nature areas, on land and at sea. It joins Special Protection Areas for birds, under the 1979 Birds Directive, with Special Areas of Conservation, under the Habitats Directive of May 1992. These sites are not fenced off from people. Many are farmed, forested or even urban. Designation is nearly complete, but management and enforcement lag, and many sites lack management plans. Its benefits are estimated at €200-300 billion a year. Developers, farmers and politicians criticize it as a brake on development, and its habitats assessment triggered the Dutch nitrogen crisis. Legal scholars also question whether its habitats test fits goals for climate and ecosystem services.

nature-pol-170.title: Point source pollution: pollution with an address
nature-pol-170.text: A factory outlet, a smokestack, a sewage plant: each is a place where pollution can be pinned down. Point source pollution is pollution of air, water, heat, noise or light that comes from a single identifiable source. The name comes from modeling, where such a source can be treated as a single mathematical point. Examples include factories, power plants, sewage treatment plants and some farms, such as large livestock feedlots ({{ref:nature-res-141}}). It contrasts with {{ref:nature-pol-075}}, which comes from wide areas such as city and farm runoff. That difference shapes policy. Direct regulation works relatively well for point sources but struggles with diffuse pollution. Large point sources such as cement factories are also where {{ref:nature-clim-185}} can capture carbon dioxide.

nature-pol-173.title: Regulatory economics: when governments set the rules
nature-pol-173.text: Should governments steer markets, or step back? Regulatory economics is the study and use of government rules to achieve economic aims, such as correcting a {{ref:nature-found-045}} or protecting the environment. Regulation is law imposed by government on people and firms to change economic behavior; some industries instead regulate themselves. Every agency is at risk of {{ref:nature-pol-040}}, being steered by the industries it oversees. Information is another problem. Principal-agent theory treats the government as the principal and the regulated firm as its agent, to deal with the firm knowing more than the regulator. Supporters, drawing on thinkers such as Karl Polanyi, argue regulation guards against monopoly, instability and environmental harm. Since regulation can counter a market failure, some economists think some rules beat an unregulated market. Others, such as Milton Friedman, George Stigler and Friedrich Hayek, argue for limiting government's role. Economists still disagree sharply on whether regulation generally improves or worsens market outcomes.

nature-pol-142.title: International environmental law: rules across borders
nature-pol-142.text: Pollution ignores borders ({{ref:nature-econ-298}}), so law has had to follow it. International environmental law is the part of international law that deals with global and regional environmental problems. It is made up of treaties, customary rules and the decisions of international courts. Most agreements are multilateral treaties, signed by many countries, and often filled out later by protocols that can add new scientific knowledge. That two-step design lets countries agree on a framework that would be too contentious if every detail had to be settled first. The {{ref:nature-clim-056}} is the best-known example. Customary rules include the duty to warn other states promptly of environmental dangers they face. One major challenge remains: setting adequate compensation for environmental damage.

nature-pol-141.title: The guiding principles of environmental law
nature-pol-141.text: Behind thousands of environmental rules sit a handful of ideas. These principles are not universally accepted, but they run through environmental law. Equity is one. {{ref:nature-eecon-224}} is the right of future generations to a fair share of the common inheritance; intragenerational equity concerns people alive today. Transboundary responsibility obliges a state to protect its own environment and prevent damage to its neighbors', which can limit its sovereign rights. Prevention is an overarching aim, served by assessing harm in advance, licensing, emission limits and the best available techniques. Precaution, as the {{ref:nature-gov-152}} puts it, means a lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective measures against serious or irreversible damage. The {{ref:nature-pol-095}} holds that the environmental costs of economic activity, including preventing harm, should fall on those who cause them rather than on society at large. Openness to the public appears in impact assessment, laws on access to environmental data, and administrative procedure.

nature-pol-160.title: Shoot, shovel and shut up: when protection backfires
nature-pol-160.text: In the American West, a grim saying sums up the worst case: 'shoot, shovel, and shut up'. The problem behind it is a perverse incentive. Strict species-protection rules can turn an endangered species into a financial burden for the landowner who hosts it. That tempts owners to destroy habitat before the species arrives. Because species could be listed under the {{ref:nature-pol-159}} without considering economic costs, the law soon became controversial. Landowners and industries face lost opportunities and delays. The evidence is more than anecdote. A 1995 study of about 1,000 private forest plots found owners more likely to harvest pines as the trees matured enough to attract endangered red-cockaded woodpeckers. Economists suggest a fix: compensate property owners for protecting species, so a listed species is no longer a potential financial loss. Cooperation can work. Agreements between landowners and the agency helped the woodpecker move from endangered to threatened by 2024. The wider argument goes on. Many hold that the protections curtail economic activity and create perverse incentives, while others defend the law's species-first approach.

nature-pol-145.title: Strategic environmental assessment: judging plans, not just projects
nature-pol-145.text: By the time a single road is assessed, the bigger choice may already have been made. Strategic environmental assessment (SEA) is a systematic process for making sure environmental, and sometimes wider sustainability, effects are considered when policies, plans and programs are drawn up. It grew from a weakness of project-level {{ref:nature-pol-132}}: many damaging choices are made earlier, such as building new infrastructure that generates more travel. An SEA usually comes before the related project assessments, so its findings cascade down and reduce later work. The EU's SEA Directive 2001/42/EC made it legally required for many regional, local, development, waste and transport plans. Its phases are screening, scoping, a baseline of the environment, estimating likely impacts, influencing the decision and monitoring afterwards. The UNECE Protocol on SEA, in force since July 2010, goes further: it can be applied to policies and legislation. Aid donors use SEA too, so that strategic-level aid considers the environment.

nature-pol-162.title: Environmental standards: the rules for treating nature
nature-pol-162.text: A pollution limit and a permit requirement have something in common. Both are environmental standards: rules, regulations or practices, usually set by government, that say how the environment must be treated and kept. Standards can ban specific activities, fix how often and how monitoring is done, or require permits to use land or water. Setting them is complex, because they rest on scientific opinion from several fields, public views and social context. Two competing views have shaped them: {{ref:nature-val-063}}, which gives nature value in itself, and {{ref:nature-val-059}}, which values it only for human survival. Practice varies. European law sets precise pollutant concentrations, plus targets to be reached by given dates. US EPA technology standards set minimum performance levels, often based on the industry's top performers, without requiring specific technologies. Some standards are voluntary: about 363,000 companies and organizations worldwide hold the ISO 14001 environmental management standard.

nature-pol-155.title: The Clean Water Act: permits for every pipe
nature-pol-155.text: In the United States, a factory may not pour waste into a river without a permit. That rule comes from the Clean Water Act, the main federal law controlling pollution of surface waters, adopted as the Federal Water Pollution Control Act Amendments of 1972. It created the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System, under which point sources such as factories and sewage plants need permits to discharge. Farm runoff and irrigation return flows were exempted as nonpoint sources. The 1972 Act also paid for municipal sewage plants, with federal grants covering 75% of project costs. Results are mixed. Its 1983 'fishable and swimmable' goal has not been met. More than half of stream and river miles, and about 70 percent of lakes, still violate water quality standards. Analysts credit it with controlling point sources but not nonpoint ones, and studies disagree on whether its benefits justify its costs.

nature-pol-147.title: Command and control: regulating by rule and penalty
nature-pol-147.text: Ten big power stations are easy to regulate. Millions of motorists are not. That contrast sums up the strengths and limits of command and control regulation. It is direct regulation by law, stating what an industry or activity may and may not do, backed by penalties for breaking the rules. The 'command' is a standard or target set by a government authority. The 'control' is the sanction for not complying, such as prosecution. This differs from using economic incentives, such as taxes and subsidies ({{ref:nature-pol-205}}), to encourage compliance. Here it relies on three main kinds of {{ref:nature-pol-162}}, usually combined. Ambient standards cover the surrounding environment, emission limits cover what a source releases, and technology standards cover its equipment. The approach dominated policy in industrial nations in the 1970s, when the focus was on remedying problems rather than broad prevention. It works fairly well for single large sources but struggles with diffuse ones. Uniform sanctions can also weigh more on small businesses than on large companies. Some commentators prefer the term 'direct regulatory instrument', because 'command and control' carries negative connotations.

nature-pol-137.title: Emission standards: legal limits on what comes out
nature-pol-137.text: Smog over Los Angeles produced the first car emission standards, enacted in the United States in 1963. Japan followed three years later. An emission standard is a legal limit on how much of a given air pollutant a particular source may release over a set period. Such standards are usually designed to achieve air quality standards and protect human life. Many target cars and other vehicles. Others cover industry, power plants and small equipment such as lawn mowers and diesel generators. Different regions and countries set different vehicle limits. Higher emission standards also help make sure efficiency gains actually cut fuel use, alongside green taxes and trading in emission permits.

nature-pol-175.title: Renewable portfolio standards: a quota for clean power
nature-pol-175.text: In 29 of 50 US states, power suppliers must by law get part of their electricity from clean sources. A renewable portfolio standard (RPS) requires electricity suppliers to get a set share of their power from renewable sources. These include wind, solar, biomass and geothermal. Certified renewable generators earn a certificate for each unit of electricity. They sell these to suppliers, who hand them to the regulator to prove compliance. Supporters say relying on the market brings competition and innovation that deliver renewable energy at the lowest cost. RPS-type schemes also exist in the UK, Italy, Poland, Sweden, Belgium and Chile. A US national laboratory credits state standards with 60% of the rise in US renewable electricity since 2000, though their share of new builds is falling. Like subsidies, these standards create protected markets for renewable energy, an alternative to {{ref:nature-pol-224}}.

nature-pol-148.title: Rules or prices? The command-and-control debate
nature-pol-148.text: Two policies can reach the same pollution target at very different costs. That claim sits at the center of a long-running argument: do direct rules or price-based tools, such as taxes and tradable permits, protect the environment more cheaply? Critics call {{ref:nature-pol-147}} inefficient. A summary of 10 studies found significant cost differences between it and least-cost alternatives. A {{ref:nature-pol-081}} shows the other logic. Instead of limiting each polluter, it lets market forces find the cheapest way to cut pollution. Enthusiasm for such incentives has grown since the 1970s, partly from disenchantment with direct rules. Defenders of direct regulation push back. Incentive schemes need monitoring and administration too, so their total costs can sometimes be higher. They often need complex rules, inspection and enforcement that make them resemble command and control. Fixed legal standards, defenders add, let regulators respond quickly to violations and give clarity to those regulated. The debate is open: economists often favor incentives as cheaper, while others argue direct rules can cost less once monitoring and administration are counted.

nature-pol-146.title: Best available technology: a standard that keeps moving
nature-pol-146.text: What counts as best keeps changing. Best available technology (BAT) is the technology or techniques that regulators approve as the standard for meeting a process's output limits, such as for pollution control. It is a moving target, because values shift and techniques advance. Read literally, it would demand the best technology regardless of cost, but in practice cost is weighed too. The idea is old. The UK's 'best practicable means' appeared in the salmon fishing law of 1861. In 1984 the EEC, forerunner of the EU, introduced 'best available techniques not entailing excessive costs'. Under today's EU Industrial Emissions Directive, BAT conclusions set the reference for permits of large industrial plants without prescribing any one technology. Under the US {{ref:nature-pol-155}}, EPA picks a model technology, sets a numeric discharge limit based on it, and lets each facility meet that limit however it chooses. BAT standards are a classic example of command and control, in contrast to {{ref:nature-pol-253}}.

nature-pol-158.title: CAFE: averaging the fuel economy of a fleet
nature-pol-158.text: The United States first enacted corporate average fuel economy (CAFE) rules in 1975, after the 1973-74 oil embargo. They require the cars and light trucks each maker sells to meet an average fuel economy. CAFE does not reward buyers or change fuel prices. It works indirectly, by penalizing automakers that build inefficient vehicles. A 2002 National Academy of Sciences report found fuel use would have been about 14 percent higher without it. But lighter vehicles may have caused 1,300 to 2,600 extra deaths in 1993. Certifying minivans and later SUVs as trucks let makers meet the less strict truck standard, helping their rise. Since 2008, targets depend on a vehicle's 'footprint', its wheelbase times track width, so makers of larger vehicles face lower targets. Efficiency also leads people to drive more: a 10% gain raises distance traveled by 1-2% on average. Critics said the fines were too small to matter, and on July 4, 2025 they were eliminated, effectively mooting the standards. Its safety effects, costs and real savings remain debated.

nature-pol-136.title: The Porter hypothesis: can tough rules make firms stronger?
nature-pol-136.text: Can a strict rule make a company stronger? In 1991 the economist Michael Porter argued that it can, and with Claas van der Linde he set out the case in a 1995 article. The Porter hypothesis holds that strict environmental regulation can push firms to become more efficient and innovative, improving their competitiveness ({{ref:nature-econ-363}}). The mechanism is the innovation effect. Regulation triggers cleaner technologies ({{ref:nature-econ-318}}) whose cost savings more than cover the costs of complying and innovating. Firms in countries that regulate early may also gain a first-mover advantage, through learning or patents. The idea is often cited in support of {{ref:nature-eecon-152}}. The evidence splits in two. Studies support a 'weak' version, that stricter regulation stimulates innovation. Evidence is mixed for the 'strong' version, that it boosts business performance. One study of OECD countries found no permanent effect of tighter environmental rules on productivity, whatever the type of regulation.

nature-pol-133.title: The environmental impact statement
nature-pol-133.text: Major US projects have been blocked in court because an agency failed to prepare an acceptable one. An environmental impact statement (EIS) is the document required under the {{ref:nature-pol-168}} for federal actions that significantly affect the quality of the human environment. It describes the good and bad environmental effects of a proposed action, and usually lists alternatives that could be chosen instead. A shorter environmental assessment comes first, to decide whether a full EIS is needed. It ends in either a Finding of No Significant Impact or an EIS.

nature-pol-143.title: Cleanup law: dealing with pollution after the fact
nature-pol-143.text: Most environmental law tries to stop pollution. Cleanup law deals with pollution that has already happened. These laws govern removing contamination from soil, sediment, surface water or groundwater. Because they respond after the fact, they must define both the needed response and who must carry it out or pay for it. Their rules may cover emergency response, sharing out liability, site assessment, remedial action, monitoring after cleanup and reuse of the site.

nature-pol-144.title: Air quality law: limits on what we breathe
nature-pol-144.text: Six pollutants sit at the center of US air law: ozone, particulate matter, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide and lead. They are the 'criteria' pollutants named for nationwide regulation. Air quality laws govern the release of pollutants into the atmosphere, mostly to protect human health. Regulators identify and classify pollutants, set limits on acceptable emissions and prescribe control technologies. Some air laws reach wider ecological problems, such as chemicals that deplete the ozone layer, or set up {{ref:nature-pol-253}} for acid rain and climate change.

nature-pol-153.title: The US Clean Air Act
nature-pol-153.text: By 2020, a 2011 EPA study projected, the Clean Air Act's 1990 amendments would cost about $60 billion a year. Their health benefits would be about $2 trillion a year. The Act is the main US federal law for preventing and reducing air pollution, first passed in 1963. The 1970 amendments created national limits on outdoor air pollution ({{ref:nature-pol-154}}), performance standards for new sources and standards for hazardous air pollutants, and strengthened federal enforcement. The 1990 amendments created the {{ref:nature-pol-262}}, the first US cap-and-trade program, to cut sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from power plants. EPA's removal of lead from gasoline, from 1971, has been called one of the great public health achievements of the 20th century. A 2022 review found overwhelming causal evidence that the Act improved air quality. After the 2007 Supreme Court ruling in Massachusetts v. EPA, and a later endangerment finding, EPA began regulating greenhouse gases. The gains are unevenly shared: ethnic-minority people are 1.5 times more likely than majority people to live in polluted areas.

nature-pol-157.title: Section 404: permits to fill wetlands
nature-pol-157.text: Before a developer can fill in a US wetland, it usually needs a permit. Section 404 of the {{ref:nature-pol-155}} requires one before dredged or fill material is placed in streams, wetlands and other regulated waters. The US Army Corps of Engineers issues them, and they are key to protecting wetlands that would otherwise be filled. Applying the rule to farming caused controversy, and the 1977 amendments added six exemptions, for activities such as normal farming. The permits also spawned a market. Wetland banking, and the 1970s policies under the Act of allowing no overall loss of wetlands, grew into {{ref:nature-mkt-120}}.

nature-pol-134.title: The case against environmental impact assessment
nature-pol-134.text: An assessment can be thorough and still miss the point. In practice almost all environmental impact assessments address only direct, immediate effects on the site itself, although the indirect effects of development can be much larger. Researchers argue that uncertainty gets too little systematic attention. Because an assessment aids decisions rather than making them, some argue its influence is limited. It can also delay environmentally friendly projects and raise their costs. Critics and practitioners still disagree about how much these studies sway decisions and how wide their scope should be.

nature-pol-135.title: Assessing harm that crosses borders
nature-pol-135.text: A project near a border can send its pollution into another country ({{ref:nature-econ-298}}). Transboundary environmental impact assessment examines effects like these. The Espoo Convention of the UN Economic Commission for Europe provides an international legal framework for it. Enforcement is hard. With no world legislature, treaties develop in parallel, which has led to duplications and failures. Even so, international advisory opinions in 2024 and 2025 confirmed that assessments must consider harm beyond national borders, including harm to the global climate system.

nature-pol-178.title: Zoning that bargains: performance and incentive zoning
nature-pol-178.text: Zoning can bargain as well as forbid. Performance zoning, first advocated by Lane Kendig in 1973, judges projects by their effects: developers may earn points for limiting environmental impacts or adding public amenities. Incentive zoning lets developers build more in return for public benefits. US cities most often use it to win mixed use, open space conservation, walkability, affordable housing and parks. Cluster zoning lets homes sit closer together, so more land stays open.

nature-pol-150.title: Can rules and penalties work for the whole planet?
nature-pol-150.text: Rules backed by sanctions need someone with the power to sanction. That is the difficulty in scaling {{ref:nature-pol-147}} up to problems that cross borders, such as the thinning ozone layer and climate change. The 1987 {{ref:nature-clim-094}} on chlorofluorocarbons is often cited as an international success for direct rules, though some see it as a special case. Climate change is often used to show the approach's failings: the problem is complex, uncertain and needs more proactive action than traditional models deliver. A blend of approaches and actors, including environmental groups, may work best.

nature-pol-149.title: The kinds of standard direct regulation uses
nature-pol-149.text: Not every rule aims at the same target. Direct regulation uses general environmental standards, target standards and performance standards. Target standards concern the receiving environment and split in two: ambient standards set goals for regulators, while receptor standards set maximum levels the regulated must not exceed. Performance standards determine what releases of a pollutant are acceptable. Which one a government uses depends on the nature of the problem and its own administrative capacity.

nature-pol-154.title: National Ambient Air Quality Standards
nature-pol-154.text: A 2025 study found that US outdoor air standards had produced more than a trillion dollars in welfare gains since 1997. The National Ambient Air Quality Standards limit the concentration in outdoor air of six pollutants that cause smog, acid rain and other health hazards. These 'criteria' pollutants are ozone, {{ref:nature-pol-068}}, lead, carbon monoxide, sulfur oxides and nitrogen oxides. Primary standards protect health. Secondary standards protect other public welfare, such as agricultural values. Areas that miss the standards become 'nonattainment areas' and must plan for 'reasonable further progress'.

nature-pol-174.title: Why regulate, and how? Two kinds of theory
nature-pol-174.text: Economists ask two questions about regulation: why does it exist, and how should it work? Positive theories answer the first, in the sense of {{ref:nature-econ-140}}. They say regulation arises to overcome information gaps ({{ref:nature-econ-330}}), to protect customers from market power, or to protect firms from rivals or from government opportunism. Normative theories answer the second. They say regulators should reduce information costs, set efficient prices, and run independent, transparent and predictable processes.

nature-pol-179.title: Performance standards and technology standards
nature-pol-179.text: A regulator can tell a factory what to achieve, or how to achieve it. Those are the two main forms of direct pollution rules. A performance standard sets a numerical emission limit for each polluter, typically measured at the discharge point, and the facility may meet it with any technology it chooses. A technology standard dictates the equipment it must use. The line blurs in practice, because regulators often base a performance standard on a model technology, as US EPA does for industrial wastewater. Examples include the US New Source Performance Standards for new industrial facilities and EU CO2 performance standards for new cars. Freedom to choose matters for cost. Letting firms pick how to meet the limit makes performance standards slightly more efficient than technology standards. Yet both are less cost-effective than {{ref:nature-pol-253}}, because the burden of cutting emissions cannot shift to firms that can cut more cheaply.

nature-pol-156.title: Two layers of discharge limits for US waters
nature-pol-156.text: The Clean Water Act sets discharge limits in two layers. The first is a national floor. Technology-based standards are set for whole categories of dischargers from what control technology can achieve, regardless of the receiving water. Congress meant them to create a 'level playing field', a basic national standard for every facility in a category. Where a water body stays polluted, stricter water-quality-based limits are added on top. These rest on water quality standards, which have four parts: designated uses, water quality criteria, an antidegradation policy and general policies.

nature-pol-138.title: Emission performance standards for power plants
nature-pol-138.text: An emission performance standard is a limit on emissions above which a different type of control technology may be needed. Such standards have capped conventional pollutants, such as nitrogen and sulfur oxides, and may also be used for carbon dioxide. Units differ by country. In the US the limit is given in pounds of carbon dioxide per megawatt-hour of electricity; elsewhere it is in kilograms per megawatt-hour.

nature-pol-139.title: Euro 4, 5, 6: Europe's vehicle emission limits
nature-pol-139.text: Every new road vehicle in the European Union must meet a set of emission limits, graded in stages such as Euro 4, Euro 5 and Euro 6. These European emission standards cover all road vehicles, trains, barges and non-road machinery such as tractors, but not seagoing ships or aircraft. A related rule, EU Regulation No 443/2009, set an average CO2 target for new cars of 130 grams per kilometer, tightened to 95 grams from 2021. The stages travel well beyond Europe. Since 2021, for example, all new vehicles in the West African ECOWAS bloc must meet Euro 4.

nature-pol-166.title: Low-emission zones: charging dirty vehicles to enter
nature-pol-166.text: London's low-emission zone, opened in 2008, was the world's largest. A low-emission zone is an area, usually in a city, where polluting vehicles are barred or charged for entering, to improve air quality. Many zones do not block entry but fine non-compliant vehicles unless a daily charge has been paid, often checked by number-plate cameras. Diesel particulates fall in most zones and health improves, often because people replace polluting vehicles with cleaner ones. As of 2019 there were about 250 such zones helping meet EU health-based air limits. The burden is uneven. People who need a car but cannot afford a cleaner one are hit hardest, so some cities enforce zones only where public transport exists, or subsidize alternatives.

nature-pol-167.title: Minimum energy performance standards for appliances
nature-pol-167.text: A refrigerator sold under these rules must hold set temperatures while using no more than a specified amount of electricity for its size and features. That is a minimum energy performance standard: a mandatory specification capping how much energy an appliance or other device may use to do a given task. It usually comes with a set test procedure, and may include non-energy requirements so that performance and user satisfaction do not suffer. California began appliance efficiency rules in 1978, and they became US national standards in 1988. Standards are often paired with energy rating labels that help buyers choose products using less energy.

nature-pol-163.title: Voluntary standards companies set for themselves
nature-pol-163.text: Some companies set environmental rules for themselves that go beyond the law. These voluntary standards usually aim to satisfy customers, governments and industry partners. Government is the strongest influence on them, followed by customers and then industry networks with codes of conduct. Skeptics abound. Companies are often said to focus on how their commitments look in advertising rather than on real implementation. Whether such self-imposed standards actually change environmental outcomes remains disputed.

nature-pol-180.title: Enforcement: making environmental rules stick
nature-pol-180.text: A rule is only as strong as its enforcement. Environmental enforcement and compliance is the work of checking whether polluters follow environmental rules and penalizing those who do not. Under the US Clean Air Act, EPA monitors compliance, seeks penalties and compels violators to comply, yet cases usually settle with penalties well below the legal maximum. Monitoring can make a market credible: the {{ref:nature-pol-262}} required continuous emissions monitoring to ensure compliance and support allowance trading. In China, strict central rules are enforced mostly by local governments more interested in economic growth. Treaties between nations on the environment are criticized for lacking monitoring and enforcement.

nature-pol-181.title: Becker's rational rule-breaker
nature-pol-181.text: Why would a firm obey a rule? Gary Becker gave an economist's answer: because breaking it does not pay. Becker applied economic reasoning to crime and other non-market behavior, assuming people act rationally. In his model, a profit-maximizing firm complies only if the expected fine exceeds the cost of complying. The expected fine is an {{ref:nature-econ-756}}: the fine weighted by the chance of being caught. The model assumes random inspection, whereas real regulators target firms more likely to be violating. The same logic predicts illicit markets wherever the expected net return from evasion beats what is available legally.

nature-pol-164.title: The Harrington paradox: why firms obey cheap-to-break rules
nature-pol-164.text: By the textbook logic, firms should break environmental rules often. Inspections are rare, violators are seldom punished, and expected fines are small next to the cost of complying. Yet most firms comply. Winston Harrington first described this puzzle in a 1988 paper based on US enforcement data from the late 1970s and early 1980s. It contradicts {{ref:nature-pol-181}}, under which a profit-maximizing firm complies only if the expected fine exceeds its compliance cost. Harrington's own explanation is targeted enforcement: regulators inspect likely violators more often, instead of choosing at random. Others point to leniency for firms that report their own violations, and to firms' altruism or concern for their self-image. Evidence is rare, and some researchers doubt the paradox exists. In Norway, most firms had minor deviations, while major violations faced strict punishment, just as Becker's theory predicts.

nature-pol-182.title: Environmental liability: making polluters owe
nature-pol-182.text: Making polluters pay requires a law that says they owe. Environmental liability is the legal responsibility of a polluter to pay for preventing and repairing the environmental damage it causes. The EU's 2004 Environmental Liability Directive, on preventing and remedying environmental damage, rests on the {{ref:nature-pol-095}}. Under US {{ref:nature-pol-176}}, liability is generally joint and several among responsible parties, so any one can be made to pay the whole bill. Sellers of land cannot pass liability for past contamination to unknowing buyers. Environmental liability insurance covers injury, property damage and cleanup costs from pollutant releases.

nature-pol-176.title: Superfund: the law that bills polluters for cleanup
nature-pol-176.text: After hazardous waste disasters such as Love Canal in New York, Congress acted in 1980. Superfund is the common name for that law, known formally as CERCLA, and its trust fund. Together they pay for cleaning up abandoned {{ref:nature-pol-054}} sites and make polluters liable for the costs. Liability is generally joint and several: each potentially responsible party can be held liable for the whole cleanup cost, then seek contributions from others. Historically about 70 percent of cleanups have been paid for by those parties. Until the mid-1990s a tax on the petroleum and chemical industries funded the trust, so polluters paid. After it lapsed, taxpayers bore most costs until a chemical tax returned in 2021. A Hazard Ranking System scores sites from 0 to 100, and a score of 28.5 puts a site on the National Priorities List for long-term cleanup. Critics blame its strict, no-fault liability for creating brownfields, as investors avoid contaminated land. Minority and low-income communities have had less chance of getting nearby sites listed and cleaned up.

nature-pol-183.title: Natural resource damage assessment: billing for injured nature
nature-pol-183.text: When a spill fouls a coast, cleanup is only part of the bill. Natural resource damage assessment is a legal process for billing nature's injuries. Public trustees measure the harm pollution has done to wildlife, waters and land, so the polluter can be made to pay for restoring them. The trustees act for the public, in the spirit of the {{ref:nature-econ-663}}. {{ref:nature-pol-176}} authorizes federal, state or tribal trustees to carry out such assessments. After the Deepwater Horizon spill, federal agencies and five Gulf states formed a trustee council, whose assessment found extensive ecological injuries across the Gulf of Mexico. A 2016 settlement included up to $8.8 billion for assessment and restoration.

nature-pol-165.title: Low-carbon fuel standards: counting from well to wheels
nature-pol-165.text: California enacted the first low-carbon fuel standard in 2007, aiming for at least a 10 percent cut in the carbon intensity of its transport fuels by 2020. Such a standard is a tradable-credit rule requiring the average carbon intensity ({{ref:nature-clim-264}}) of a region's transport fuels to fall below that of gasoline and diesel. It counts emissions over the fuel's whole life cycle, 'well to wheels', not just from the tailpipe ({{ref:nature-acct-050}}). Whether to count emissions from indirect land-use change caused by biofuels was fiercely debated. Scientists and the biofuel industry disagreed over whether they could be estimated well enough to include. Canada requires liquid fossil fuel suppliers to cut carbon intensity to 15% below 2016 levels by 2030.

nature-pol-172.title: Pollution prevention: not making it in the first place
nature-pol-172.text: Pollution that is never made needs no cleanup. Pollution prevention is a strategy of cutting the amount of waste created in the first place, rather than treating it after release, especially by industry, farms and consumers. Many large corporations see it as a way to make production more efficient and profitable, through less waste and better technology. In the United States it was written into law through the Pollution Prevention Act of 1990 and the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments.

nature-pol-171.title: Regulating and monitoring pollution
nature-pol-171.text: Behind every pollution limit stand an agency and a measurement. Regulation and monitoring of pollution means the laws and agencies that limit pollution and reduce its harm, together with the measuring of pollution levels. Locally, environmental agencies or the public health system usually oversee it. The modern system began with US rules on industrial and mining air and water pollution in the 1960s and 1970s. Because many pollutants cross borders, UN treaties regulate them too, such as the {{ref:nature-clim-094}} of 1987 on ozone-depleting chemicals. Polluters have historically lobbied governments of poorer countries to keep regulation lax.
